title: A Short History of Money
author: Barashada Ingiriisiga
description: From cowrie shells to contactless cards, this book tells the surprising story of how money was invented, why it keeps changing, and how each new form reshaped power, trust, and daily life.

chapters.title: The World Before Money
chapters.text:
Imagine for a moment that you want to buy a loaf of bread. You walk into a shop, hand over a few coins or a card, and leave with your purchase. The whole process takes seconds, and you rarely stop to think about it. You trust that the shopkeeper will accept your payment, and the shopkeeper trusts that those coins or digits on a screen have real value. This trust is so deep that we forget it exists at all. Yet money is not a natural thing. It was invented, changed, and reinvented many times over thousands of years, and its story begins long before the first coin was ever struck.

To understand how money began, we have to travel back to a time before written records, before cities, before farming. Early human societies lived in small groups, moving with the seasons to follow animals and gather plants. In these groups, survival depended on cooperation. People shared food, tools, and skills because their lives depended on one another. A skilled hunter might bring back a deer, and the whole group would eat. A woman who knew which plants were safe to eat would share that knowledge freely. In this world, there was no exchange in the way we understand it today. There was simply giving, and the expectation that others would give in return when the need arose. This is what scholars call a gift economy.

The gift economy worked well in small, close communities. Everyone knew everyone else. If someone failed to share when they had plenty, the group would remember, and that person would lose trust and respect. Reputation acted as a kind of social glue. But this system had serious limits. It depended on people knowing each other personally and on a shared sense of obligation. As populations grew and groups came into contact with strangers, the simple logic of giving and receiving began to break down. How could you trust someone you had never met? How could you be sure that a promise would be kept across a distance of many miles?

This is where barter enters the story. Barter means the direct exchange of goods and services without any medium of exchange. A farmer with too much grain might trade with a neighbour who had extra sheep. A potter might swap her bowls for a pair of shoes. At first glance, barter seems simple and fair. But it had a fundamental problem that historians and economists call the double coincidence of wants. For a trade to happen, both parties had to want exactly what the other was offering, at exactly the same time, and in exactly the right amounts. Imagine a fisherman who needed new arrows. He could find a maker of arrowheads, but what if the arrowhead maker did not want fish? The fisherman would have to find someone else who wanted fish and who had something the arrowhead maker wanted. This chain of trades could go on for a long time. It was slow, frustrating, and often impossible.

There were other problems too. Some goods were difficult to divide. A cow, for example, could not easily be cut into pieces for a small purchase. Other goods spoiled quickly. A basket of fruit might rot before a suitable trade partner was found. And how could anyone compare the value of very different things? Was a clay pot worth more or less than a pair of sandals? Without a common measure, every trade was a difficult negotiation. Barter was not impossible, but it was inefficient. It could work in emergencies or between strangers, but it could not support a growing, complex society.

Because of these limitations, human societies began to choose certain objects to serve as a common measure of worth. These objects were not money in the modern sense, but they were the ancestors of money. They had to be things that many people valued, that were hard to fake, and that could be stored and carried. Different cultures chose different things, depending on their environment and their needs.

In many parts of the world, cattle became a standard of value. A cow or a bull was useful in many ways. It provided milk, meat, and leather, and it could pull a plough. Cattle were also mobile, which meant they could be moved from place to place. In some ancient languages, the word for cattle and the word for wealth were the same. The Latin word pecunia, which means money, comes from pecus, meaning cattle. This shows how deeply animals were connected to the idea of value. But cattle had their own problems. They could die of disease, they needed food and water, and they were difficult to divide. You could not easily pay for a small item with half a cow.

Salt was another early form of value. In hot climates, salt was essential for preserving meat and fish, and human bodies need it to survive. Salt was produced in certain places and had to be carried long distances, which made it precious. Roman soldiers were sometimes paid in salt, and the English word salary comes from the Latin word salarium, which originally meant a payment of salt. This connection between salt and payment shows how important this simple mineral was.

Shells also played a major role in the history of money. Cowrie shells, in particular, were used across Africa, Asia, and the Pacific islands for thousands of years. They were small, durable, easy to count, and difficult to fake. They could be strung together like beads and carried in large numbers. Their beauty made them desirable, and their scarcity in inland areas gave them value. The use of shells shows an important idea: money does not have to be made of metal or paper. It just has to be something that people agree to accept.

What all these early forms of value had in common was trust. A cow was valuable because everyone in the community accepted that it was valuable. Salt was valuable because everyone needed it and knew that others needed it too. This trust was local. It worked within a community or a region, but it did not travel easily. A person from the coast who carried cowrie shells inland might find that the farmers there had never seen them and did not want them. Value was not universal. It was shaped by place, by culture, and by circumstance.

As societies grew larger and trade routes stretched across continents, the limits of these early systems became more obvious. People needed something that could be trusted by strangers, something that could be measured and counted precisely, something that did not spoil or die. The answer, when it came, was metal. But before metal coins appeared, there was another step. People began to weigh and measure precious metals like gold and silver. These metals were rare, beautiful, and resistant to rust and decay. They could be melted down and formed into bars or rings. Their value could be checked by weighing them. But even this was not enough. Every trade still required a scale, and every trader had to trust the weight and the purity of the metal. The idea of money was taking shape, but it still lacked a crucial element: a guarantee.

That guarantee would come with the invention of coins, stamped by an authority that everyone trusted. But that is the story of the next chapter. For now, it is enough to understand the world before money. It was a world of gifts and obligations, of barter and its frustrations, of cattle and salt and shells. It was a world where value was real but local, where trust was personal, and where the exchange of goods was always a human act. Money did not fall from the sky. It grew slowly out of human needs and human relationships, one small step at a time.

chapters.title: The Age of Metal and Coins
chapters.text:
The move from cattle, salt, and other early forms of money to metal was not sudden, nor was it obvious at the time. For thousands of years, people had relied on objects that had clear practical uses. A cow could feed a family, and salt could preserve meat. But these forms of money had serious weaknesses. Cattle were heavy, slow, and needed constant care. Salt could be ruined by rain or lost in transit. Most importantly, neither could be divided easily. You could not cut a cow in half to buy a smaller item, and you could not easily measure the exact value of a handful of salt against a piece of cloth.

Metals offered a solution to these problems, but not all metals were equal. Iron and copper were common in many regions, yet their value was low and their quality varied from place to place. Gold and silver, however, had a special appeal. They did not rust or decay. They could be melted down and reshaped without losing their purity. They were rare enough to hold value in small amounts, yet heavy enough to feel substantial in the hand. A small piece of gold could represent a great deal of wealth, which made it perfect for long journeys and large transactions. For the first time, value could be carried in a pocket rather than driven across a field.

The problem with raw metal, though, was trust. If you offered someone a lump of silver, how could they know it was truly silver and not a mixture of cheaper metals? How could they know its weight was honest? These questions slowed trade and created constant arguments. The solution came from an unexpected place: the kingdom of Lydia, in what is now Turkey, around the year 600 BCE. The Lydians began to produce small, uniform pieces of a natural mixture of gold and silver called electrum. Each piece was stamped with a design, usually a lion, which served as a guarantee from the king. The stamp said: this piece contains this much metal, and it is genuine.

This was a revolutionary idea. The coin was not valuable because of what it could do, but because of what it represented. The stamp was a promise, and the king's authority stood behind that promise. If the king was strong and respected, his coins were accepted far beyond his borders. Merchants from other lands learned to recognise the lion symbol and knew they could trust it. This trust was the true invention. The metal was simply the messenger.

At roughly the same time, a very different coinage system was developing in China. The Chinese did not use gold and silver as their primary materials. Instead, they cast coins from bronze, often in the shape of small knives or spades, which reflected their agricultural past. These early Chinese coins were not stamped with a royal seal in the same way as the Lydian coins. They were produced in large quantities and circulated widely within the empire, but their value was tied more to their official status than to their metal content. The bronze itself was not worth very much; it was the authority of the state that gave the coin its purchasing power. This difference between East and West would have lasting consequences. In the West, coins were valued for their metal content first, and their official stamp second. In the East, the official stamp was everything.

As coins spread across the Mediterranean and beyond, they changed the nature of trade. Long-distance commerce had always been risky. A merchant travelling from one city to another could not be certain that the goods he carried would be accepted, or that the payment he received would be worth anything when he returned home. Coins solved this problem in a way that no earlier form of money had managed. Because coins were standardised, a merchant could calculate the value of his cargo before he set out. He knew exactly how many coins he would need to buy a certain quantity of olive oil or a roll of fine cloth. This predictability reduced risk, and reduced risk encouraged more trade.

But there was a darker side to this new system. The power to mint coins was a source of enormous political strength, and governments were quick to recognise it. Whoever controlled the coinage controlled the economy. A ruler could decide to reduce the amount of precious metal in his coins, keeping the same design but using cheaper materials. This practice, known as debasement, allowed a government to produce more coins without finding more gold or silver. At first, this seemed like a clever way to increase wealth. But the merchants who received the coins quickly noticed that they felt lighter or looked different. When trust in a coin collapsed, so did its value, and prices would rise sharply. Inflation was born.

The temptation to debase the currency was almost irresistible, and it led to a constant battle between rulers and their subjects. A wise ruler understood that his coins were only as strong as his reputation. If he kept the metal content honest, his coins would be accepted widely and trade would flourish, bringing him tax revenue from the growing economy. A greedy or desperate ruler, however, would debase the coins to pay for wars or palaces, only to discover that the resulting inflation destroyed the very wealth he had hoped to gain. This tension between short-term gain and long-term trust became a central theme in the history of money.

Standardisation also changed the relationship between citizens and the state. When coins were uniform, taxes could be collected in a consistent way. A farmer no longer had to bring a portion of his harvest to the local lord; he could sell his crops and pay his taxes in coin. This may seem like a small change, but it had deep effects. It meant that the state no longer needed to store vast quantities of grain or livestock. It meant that wealth could be measured, counted, and compared in a way that was impossible with cattle or salt. It also meant that the state knew exactly how much money was circulating, and could plan its spending accordingly. Taxation became more efficient, but it also became more impersonal. The relationship between ruler and subject was no longer based on gifts and obligations, but on numbers and payments.

By the time the Roman Empire rose to power, coins had become the backbone of the Mediterranean economy. The Roman denarius, a small silver coin, was accepted from Britain to Egypt, and its design carried the image of the emperor, reminding every user of who held authority. The coins of Rome were not just money; they were a form of communication. They spread the emperor's face across the known world and reinforced the idea that his power was universal. Yet even Rome could not escape the consequences of debasement. As the empire faced military pressures, emperors reduced the silver content of the denarius again and again, and each reduction eroded public confidence. By the time the western empire fell, its coins were worth a fraction of what they had once been, and the trust that had held the system together had vanished.

The age of metal and coins taught humanity a difficult lesson. Money is not simply a useful tool; it is a promise. That promise can be kept or broken, and its fate depends on the character of those who hold power. The invention of coins made trade faster, fairer, and more widespread than ever before. It allowed distant communities to connect in ways that were previously impossible. But it also gave governments a new kind of power, the power to shape value itself. That power could build empires or destroy them, and it has never left the hands of those who control the money supply. The coins of Lydia are long gone, but the questions they raised about trust, authority, and value remain as urgent today as they were two and a half thousand years ago.

chapters.title: Paper, Banks, and Promises
chapters.text:
For centuries, the value of money seemed to depend on the material it was made from. A gold coin was worth something because it contained a certain amount of gold. You could hold it in your hand, weigh it, and even test its quality by biting it. But coins had serious problems. They were heavy to carry in large quantities, and travelling merchants were always at risk of being robbed. In a world of slow roads and unreliable law, keeping your wealth safe was a constant worry.

In seventeenth-century England, a solution began to take shape in an unexpected place: the goldsmith's workshop. Goldsmiths worked with precious metals every day, and they had strong locks and secure storerooms. Merchants and wealthy citizens started to leave their gold coins with these goldsmiths for safekeeping. In return, the goldsmith issued a receipt, a written promise that the gold was safe and would be returned on demand. At first, these receipts were simply a form of proof. When you wanted your gold back, you presented the receipt and received your coins.

Soon, however, people discovered something useful. When buying a valuable item, instead of going to fetch their coins, they could simply hand over the goldsmith's receipt. The seller knew that the goldsmith was reliable)Skip: the receipt was trusted, so it worked as a form of payment. As long as people believed the promise on the paper, the paper itself became valuable. This was a revolutionary idea. Money no longer had to be a physical object like a coin; it could be a promise, printed on paper. The goldsmith quickly realised that most customers never came back for their gold all at once. The coins simply sat in the strongroom, unused. So the goldsmith began lending out some of this gold to other people, charging them interest. He kept the promise to return the gold on demand, but he acted as a banker, and in doing so, he created something even more important: credit.

These early experiments were not unique to Europe. In fact, paper money had appeared in China many centuries earlier. During the Tang dynasty, merchants used something similar to receipts for deposits of goods and coinscarin. But it was under the Song dynasty, around the eleventh century, that the government began printing official paper money to solve a problem. China had a population of over one hundred million, and its economy was growing rapidly. There was simply not enough copper or silver to mint enough coins for all transactions. Paper could be produced more quickly and cheaply, and it was much lighter to carry. For several centuries, this system worked wellcars. Chinese paper money was widely accepted and made trade easier than anywhere else in the world.

Yet the Chinese experiment also revealed a great danger. For a piece of paper to act as money, people must believe that the promise behind it will be honoured. When the government printed too much paper money to pay for wars and palace expenses, the value of each note fell as more were produced. People lost confidence. Prices rose, and the paper money became almost worthless. By the fifteenth century, the government abandoned paper money entirely and returned to coins. The lesson was clear: if trust is broken, money collapses.

In Europe, banks learned the same lesson in a different way. In the eighteenth century, a banknote was still essentially a promise to pay the holder a fixed amount in gold. But banks also created money out of nothing, in a sense, by lending. When a bank lent fifty pounds to a baker, it did not always hand over fifty gold coins. It opened an account with fifty pounds in it, in writing. The baker could write a note instructing the bank to pay his supplier. That supplier might deposit the note in his own account. In this way, money existed not as coins but as entries in a ledger, a simple record of numbers. The total amount of money in the economy had grown, even though no new gold had been dug out of the ground.

This was the birth of modern banking. The key to the whole system was confidence. A bank could make loans and create money because it knew that only a small fraction of depositors would ask for their money back at any one time. This works well in normal conditions. If people believe their money is safe, they keep it in the bank, and the system continues to function. But if rumours spread that a bank has made too many bad loans, everyone races to withdraw their money at once. This is called a bank run, and it has destroyed many banks throughout history. In a bank run, the bank does not have enough physical money to pay everyone because it has lent most of it out. The promise breaks, and the bank fails. The truth is that banking rests on a fragile foundation: the shared belief that tomorrow will be like today.

As time passed, governments took control of this system. They created central banks to issue paper money and to supervise private banks. A single printed note, issued by a national bank, was easier to trust than notes from many small private banks, each with a different reputation. Slowly, the right to print money became a central tool of state power. In China, the state controlled the printing directly. In Europe, a working partnership developed between governments and private financiers. Governments needed money to build roads, fight wars, and pay officials, and banks were able to lend them vast sums far beyond the gold they actually held.

This transformation changed how people understood money itself. For most of human history, money was an object: a cow, a shell, a coin. By the nineteenth century, money had become something more abstract. It was a promise, a debt, an entry in a book. A banknote was valuable not because of its paper but because of the system of trust behind it. Every time you accept a note or a payment, you are agreeing to participate in that shared belief.

Today, most money does not exist in physical form at all. It is simply numbers in computers, moved between accounts with electronic signals. Yet the principle is exactly the same as the goldsmith's receipt. Money is a promise we all agree to trust. Our modern economy is built on that trust, and it is far more powerful, and far more fragile, than a bag of gold coins could ever be.

chapters.title: Central Banks and Economic Trust
chapters.text:
For most of human history, money was tied to things people could see and touch. Coins contained silver or gold. Paper notes could be exchanged for those metals at a bank counter. Trust in money meant trust in a physical object. But as economies grew larger and more interconnected, that simple trust no longer seemed sufficient. Governments began to understand that money was too important to be left entirely in the hands of private banks. From this idea, a new institution was born: the central bank.

The first true central bank appeared in England at the end of the seventeenth century. In 1694, the Bank of England was created to lend money to the government, which needed funds for war. In return, the bank received special privileges, including the right to issue paper notes. At first, it was just one bank among many. Gradually, however, it took on a unique role. It became the government's banker Tree optimization: and, later, the banker to other banks. When smaller banks faced difficulties, they could borrow from the Bank of England to survive. This function became known as the role of "lender of last resort." Its purpose was to prevent a single bank's failure from spreading panic through the whole financial system. This idea was simple but powerful: if people believed that a strong institution stood behind the banks, they would keep their money where it was.

Of course, for most of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, paper money still needed a firm physical anchor. Under the gold standard, a government promised to exchange its currency for a fixed amount of gold at any time and opened its doors to the public. This promise limited rulers in a way that earlier kings and queens had rarely faced. In the past, a ruler could reduce the amount of metal in the currency, or simply replace old coins with lighter ones, to gain more money at the expense of the people. The gold standard made such tricks much harder. A country could only issue as much paper money as its gold supplies allowed, and international trade benefited from the confidence this created. In ordinary times, the gold standard was a machine for producing trust. In extraordinary times, however, it proved too rigid.

This rigidity was exposed during the First World War. To fund the conflict, governments suspended the gold standard and printed money in enormous amounts. The result was inflation, and the poor and the middle class saw their savings lose value almost weekly. In Germany, hyperinflation made this experience extremely painful: people rushed to spend their wages before the prices changed again, and the entire idea of a reliable store of value disappeared. A waiter's tip was worth more than a fortune saved in government bonds. The memory of that time taught lawmakers everywhere that economic trust is a precious thing. If money becomes meaningless, so do contracts, wages, and hopes for the future. Social order itself can seem fragile.

Economic trust, then, has never been simply about metal or paper. It is built on institutions, promises, and self-control. Governments and central banks earn credibility when they act predictably over long periods. They lose it quickly when they print money without limit or allow banks to collapse without protection. The history of money is not only a history of coins and notes. It is also a history of how societies decide who can be trusted with value on a national scaleukan.

A central bank that helps other banks in financial trouble
A bank that only lends to governments
A bank that prints paper money
questions.explanation: The text explains: 'When smaller banks faced difficulties, they could borrow from the Bank of England to survive. This function became known as the role of "lender of last resort."'

questions.question: What was the gold standard according to the chapter?
options: A promise to exchange paper currency for a fixed amount of gold
A system where only gold coins were used as money
A rule requiring banks to hold gold in their vaults
A method of printing money backed by gold reserves
questions.explanation: The text states: 'Under the gold standard, a government promised to exchange its currency for a fixed amount of gold at any time.'

questions.question: What happened to the gold standard during the First World War?
options: It was strengthened to support the war effort
It was suspended so governments could print more money
It became more flexible with new rules
It was replaced by a silver standard
questions.explanation: The text says: 'To fund the conflict, governments suspended the gold standard and printed money in enormous amounts.'

questions.question: What does 'hyperinflation' mean as described in the chapter?
options: A slow and steady increase in prices
A very rapid and extreme increase in prices
A decrease in the general price level
A period of stable prices with no change
questions.explanation: The text describes hyperinflation in Germany: 'people rushed to spend their wages before the prices changed again' and 'A waiter's tip was worth more than a fortune saved in government bonds.'

questions.question: What lesson did lawmakers learn from the German hyperinflation experience?
options: Economic trust is a precious thing
The gold standard should never be abandoned
Banks should be privately owned and unregulated
Printing more money is the best way to fund wars
questions.explanation: The text concludes: 'The memory of that time taught lawmakers everywhere that economic trust is a precious thing.'

chapters.title: Digital Money and the Future
chapters.text:
The twentieth century ended with a strange paradox. Money, in the minds of most people, still meant coins and banknotes, the familiar weight in a pocket or wallet. Yet the real business of finance had long since moved beyond paper. Cheques had been common for over a century, but the true revolution was the credit card. Introduced widely in the 1950s and 1960s, the card changed the relationship between the buyer, the seller, and the bank. Instead of handing over physical value, the cardholder signed a promise to pay later. The seller trusted the bank to settle the debt. The consumer trusted the card to be accepted anywhere. A small plastic rectangle had become a symbol of worldwide trust. In this sense, the digital future had already begun, although no one yet called it that.

The older systems moved information, but they were slow. A cheque might take days to move, journeying by post or courier between banks in different cities or countries. The final transfer of value could not be confirmed until the paper physically reached its destination. Credit cards were faster to use but slower to settle. There was still too much that depended on objects: paper slips, signatures, printed statements. The great transformation of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries was to remove the objects entirely. Money, in the words of one economist, became pure information. The money in your account was not stored anywhere, not in a vault, not as notes beside your name. It was just numbers in a database. When money moved, the numbers changed. Nothing physically travelled.

Smartphones accelerated this change beyond what most experts had imagined. In many parts of Europe and Africa, and especially in Asia, people began paying with a touch of the device. Mobile payment systems, built on apps and messaging services, allowed people to send value instantly, if they had no bank account. In parts of East Africa, mobile money became far more common than traditional banking. Small crops grown by farmers, taxi rides, school fees from children, all of these were settled through mobile accounts. The trust of account moved from the bank branch to the network, acceptance to a phone signal. Anybody with access to electricity and a signal could join the system, creating value from experience. For the first time, an identity matched barriers to trust in many poor communities, because here the machine calculated the status of each person.

This new world of everyday trust existed alongside a far bolder experiment. In 2009, an unknown person or group introduced Bitcoin, which they claimed was the first truly digital form of money. The coins were not issued by any government, nor supported by any bank. Instead, they existed only in a public, shared record called the blockchain. Every transaction was recorded forever in the digital copy of the record held by every user. No single authority could change erase or rule it. This was money created purely by code, confirmed by the network of its own users. Its anonymous founder released it quietly and disappeared.

At first, Bitcoin seemed like a curiosity for technology lovers. But as its value rose and fell with startling force, it attracted attention. It also attracted intense argument. Supporters saw it as a way to escape government control, because no central bank could print more Bitcoins to save political goals. They claimed it gave power back to the individual. Critics answered that exchange rates were so unstable that the currency replaced trust with anxiety. A shop owner in Vancouver who accepted it one morning might find the payment worth less by lunch. Money was supposed to be the stable measure of value, that was its whole purpose. If an object of exchange could not hold its value steadily, could it truly be recognised as money in remembered sense? Some said this was not money at all, but apparently a speculative asset, a digital gold without the gold.

Governments had always guarded a privilege: the power to create and control money. Cryptocurrencies would force them to respond. The first response was a warning. Nations debated whether to ban these currencies or to simply permit them but not treat them as legal money. The second response was far more important, and it continues to unfold: the development of the central bank digital currency, or CBDC. This idea unfolds the digital money but with a crucial difference. It would, as the names suggest, be issued by the central bank and supported by the national state, just like the physical money we all know. In practical terms, a citizen might open a digital wallet provided by the central bank. This wallet would hold digital money that could be spent instantly, with no need for a commercial bank in between.

The promise of such a system is simple: fast payments, lower costs, and financial inclusion for millions of people who still have no bank account. Trust would be absolute, because the same government that had issued the currency and collected taxes would be the one supporting the digital euro or pound or dollar. The end, it would seem, of the history of the interruption of the commercial bank between the citizen and the money supply was removed.

But the idea raised uncomfortable questions. If there is a digital currency, then every transaction might be visible to the state, and governments would have a second view of their citizens finances. Privacy, a careful exercise by many generations, would be easily dissolved. A national economy could be monitored, measured, and directed with greater precision than ever before. Then there is the question of power. The central bank could, in theory, control precisely how much money someone could spend, and decide whether to freeze a digital wallet instantly. Trust in a government disappears when a citizen fears to spend. No coin or note provides the same silence; a bad decision to use a digital system could function with far more force than a decision about tax.

At this point, the fundamental nature of money is being examined again. Money has always existed through trust. The first coins were trusted because of their gold content; later, notes trusted because of the signature and the bank; digital money trusted because of the software, the algorithm, or the state. In other centuries, humans slowly built layers of trust, moving from one form to another, always looking for a more efficient exchange, a better measure of stability. The newest technologies offer tremendous promise: innovation from smartphones packaged, and savings in an app. Individuals gained new abilities. Yet the old fear returns as people wonder about the once simple goals. Who will be trusted with money's record? Who will be able to revoke a digital payments that is not physically possible? And when the systems fail, to whom do we turn? Through centuries of exchange, these questions have been asked and answered, by coins, by banks, and by promises. Now, in the digital world, we are asking them again. There is no reason to believe the answer will be simpler. Money was always a fragile form of trust; the future, it seems, will make us trust not only one another, but the code as well.

questions.question: What does the author suggest about the nature of money in the modern era?
options: Money is still primarily physical.
Money has become more digital.
Money is only backed by gold.
Money is controlled by private banks.
questions.explanation: The text shows the progression from physical to digital, stating 'the digital future had already begun' early on and describing how money became information.

questions.question: What is the meaning of 'paradox' as used in the first sentence?
options: A contradiction that is true.
A simple solution.
A financial transaction.
A type of currency.
questions.explanation: A paradox is a statement that seems contradictory but may be true; here, money is still seen as physical but actually digital.

questions.question: How does Bitcoin differ from traditional government-issued money?
options: It is issued by a central bank.
It is not backed by any government.
It is only used in Africa.
It is made of metal coins.
questions.explanation: The text says Bitcoin 'were not issued by any government, nor supported by any bank.'

questions.question: According to the text, what is a major criticism of Bitcoin?
options: It is too slow.
Its value is unstable.
It is controlled by banks.
It requires physical delivery.
questions.explanation: Critics answer that 'exchange rates were so unstable that the currency replaced trust with anxiety.'

questions.question: What does 'fragile' mean in the context of the last paragraph?
options: Easily broken or damaged.
Very strong.
Heavy and solid.
Transparent.
questions.explanation: Fragile means easily broken; the text says 'Money was always a fragile form of trust.'

questions.question: What is the promise of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) as mentioned?
options: They will replace cash entirely.
They offer fast payments, lower costs, and financial inclusion.
They are anonymous and unregulated.
They are backed by gold.
questions.explanation: The text says CBDCs promise 'fast payments, lower costs, and financial inclusion for millions of people who still have no bank account.'

vocabulary.definition: A statement that contradicts itself but might be true.
Easily broken or damaged; delicate.
A dramatic and wide-reaching change in the way something works or is organized.
Confidence in the reliability or truth of something or someone.

writing_prompt.prompt: Think about the forms of money you have used in your life, from coins and banknotes to mobile transfers and cards. Has your trust in money ever been tested, for example during inflation or a payment failure? Describe how your personal experience compares to the historical changes described in this book.
